title: String B: the cable from B01 to the substation
about: The running case for HV Subsea Cable Testing, a refresher in the format Dan approved for Design and verification (format/refresher.md there). A made-up commissioning job: every given is cited to Dan's notes (notes p.N, the PDF page), marked as a practice value, or marked as a typical value research must quote. Every figure is worked by a script from the inputs shown with it. Items marked ➕ in his notes are background to check, not sources.
rounding: Each figure is worked from the inputs shown with it, rounded half up: currents, energies and resistances in mΩ to 2 decimal places (3 where the notes print 3), voltages in kV and distances in m to 1, ratios to 2. A typed answer is accepted within "accept" where given.

cites.notes: source/subsea-cable-testing-notes.pdf, PDF page (Dan's own notes, 10 pages)
cites.practice value: made up for the running case; said so on screen
cites.to research: a typical value the research stage must quote word for word before a lesson uses it

scenario.title: String B: the cable from B01 to the substation
scenario.text: Commissioning tests on a newly laid 66 kV inter-array cable on an offshore wind farm. It runs 2.40 km from turbine B01 to the offshore substation (OSS), the last cable of string B. Three-core, 3 × 240 mm² copper, XLPE, 38/66 (72.5) kV, copper wire screens, armoured, with one field joint 1620 m from the OSS. A technician at each end, talking before every change. The live string A runs in the same corridor. One fault waits to be found. Every figure is a practice value unless it is cited.
scenario.source: A practice job, made up for this course; the test methods and limits are from Dan's notes.

givens.label: Absorption time constant of the IR curve (interactive model)
givens.cite: practice value (the running case is made up for practice; no real wind farm); drives the curve in the lesson 3 picture only: 1/R(t) = 1/R∞ + A × e^(−t/τ), where 1/R∞ is the steady leakage and A the absorption. Fitted through the 30 s and 1 min readings, it lands within 7 per cent of the 10 min readings: L1 R∞ 63.7 GΩ (model gives 63.6 GΩ at 10 min against the 62 GΩ read); L2 R∞ 2.4 GΩ (model gives 2.4 GΩ at 10 min against the 2.4 GΩ read); L3 R∞ 55.7 GΩ (model gives 55.7 GΩ at 10 min against the 60 GΩ read). The picture marks the case readings themselves. Moisture adds to the steady leakage and nothing else. No standard gives a τ; the real one differs with every cable.

assumptions.label: Copper's resistance rises 0.00393 of its 20 °C value per °C
assumptions.why: Linear rule R_t = R20 × (1 + 0.00393 × (t − 20)). The notes say about 0.4% per °C; Quoted: the standard temperature coefficient of copper is 0.00393 per °C at 20 °C (NIST copper wire tables, research source 210), and IEC 60228 has the measured resistance corrected to 20 °C by the factors in its Table A.1 (source 211). The linear form is the course's own working from that coefficient.
assumptions.text: Assumed: Copper's resistance rises 0.00393 of its 20 °C value per °C. Linear rule R_t = R20 × (1 + 0.00393 × (t − 20)). The notes say about 0.4% per °C; Quoted: the standard temperature coefficient of copper is 0.00393 per °C at 20 °C (NIST copper wire tables, research source 210), and IEC 60228 has the measured resistance corrected to 20 °C by the factors in its Table A.1 (source 211). The linear form is the course's own working from that coefficient.

assumptions.label: Phase ID: each core is tested to the screen in turn, with only that core joined to the screen at the far end
assumptions.why: The notes say the cable is earthed at both ends to start, with conductor and screen disconnected and a technician at each end, and that each core is proved by a core-to-screen continuity test from both ends (p.2). A utility's procedure tests each conductor in turn using the screen as the return (research: SSEN 9.1). No source found gives the earthing order, so the lesson assumes: every core earthed at both ends to start; the far end keeps one core joined to the screen through its earth and lifts the other two under control; your end lifts its earths under control and tests each core to the screen, and only the joined core reads continuity; the earths go back on, and the ends swap.

assumptions.label: The 'charging time' in the 5× discharge rule is the time the test voltage was applied
assumptions.why: The notes do not define it. Megger's guide to testing above 1 kV says to discharge the item for five times as long as it was tested and gives the example: after a 10-minute PI test, allow the unit to discharge for 50 minutes (research source 223). A Fluke application note says the discharge time should be about five times the testing charge time (source 222). The same Megger guide also uses 'charging time' for the time a test set takes to charge the sample, a separate figure that depends on capacitance (source 224). Megger's older guide gives about four times (source 107): the lesson uses five.
assumptions.text: Sourced: the charging time in the 5× rule is the time the test voltage was applied. The notes do not define it. A Fluke application note says the discharge time should be about five times the testing charge time (source 222). The same Megger guide also uses 'charging time' for the time a test set takes to charge the sample, a separate figure that depends on capacitance (source 224). Megger's older guide gives about four times (source 107): the lesson uses five.

assumptions.label: The tests run in the order of the notes' test sequence
assumptions.why: Phase ID, core resistance, IR with PI and DAR, sheath, VLF, then LIRA (notes p.9, added background). TDR comes in when the VLF test breaks down.
assumptions.text: Assumed: The tests run in the order of the notes' test sequence. Phase ID, core resistance, IR with PI and DAR, sheath, VLF, then LIRA (notes p.9, added background). TDR comes in when the VLF test breaks down.

assumptions.label: The client asks for the VLF test on all three cores despite L2's sheath result
assumptions.why: A story choice so one fault shows up in four tests. On a real job the engineer stops and reports first (notes p.10: figure out why before submitting).

assumptions.label: The core oversheaths are semi-conductive
assumptions.why: So the positive lead goes to the sheath's semi-con layer through the roll spring (notes p.4). Read it off the cable data sheet.
assumptions.text: Assumed: The core oversheaths are semi-conductive. So the positive lead goes to the sheath's semi-con layer through the roll spring (notes p.4). Read it off the cable data sheet.

assumptions.label: The sheath test is made on each core's own oversheath
assumptions.why: A three-core 66 kV array cable has a polyethylene sheath on each power core (research source 253); the armour and the polypropylene yarn serving sit outside the three cores (source 254) and are open to seawater, so the case does not test them. No source found says how the outer electrode is made on a subsea cable on site: the case uses the notes' two methods (roll spring on a semi-conductive sheath, earth electrode on an insulating one) and a.semicon.
assumptions.text: Assumed: The sheath test is made on each core's own oversheath. A three-core 66 kV array cable has a polyethylene sheath on each power core (research source 253); the armour and the polypropylene yarn serving sit outside the three cores (source 254) and are open to seawater, so the case does not test them. No source found says how the outer electrode is made on a subsea cable on site: the case uses the notes' two methods (roll spring on a semi-conductive sheath, earth electrode on an insulating one) and a.semicon.

assumptions.label: Worst case trapped charge: switched off at the peak of U0
assumptions.why: A de-energised cable can be left charged. The case works the most it could hold. Sourced: 'trapped charge' left on the capacitance of equipment, for example after insulation resistance testing a length of cable (IET Wiring Matters, research source 186); high-voltage cables are to be treated as capacitors that store energy (source 188); E = ½CV² (source 191). The peak-of-U0 worst case itself is the course's own.

assumptions.label: The TDR velocity is set from the known route length
assumptions.why: The open-end reflection and the 2.40 km installation record give v (Megger TDR_AN58: test a known length and adjust the VF).
assumptions.text: Assumed: The TDR velocity is set from the known route length. The open-end reflection and the 2.40 km installation record give v (Megger TDR_AN58: test a known length and adjust the VF).

assumptions.label: The lesson teaches PI as the notes do, though String B's 1-minute readings are far above 5000 MΩ
assumptions.why: IEEE 43 (a rotating-machine practice, quoted through AEMC, research source 233) does not recommend PI as an assessment tool when the 1-minute reading is above 5000 MΩ. L1 reads 24 GΩ and L3 23 GΩ at 1 minute. The notes and Megger apply PI to cables with no such limit, and Fluke says cabling shows little absorption current (source 238). The lesson works PI on the case readings as the notes teach it, says the high reading makes the ratio less trustworthy, and tells him the client's criterion and the trend settle the matter. The readings are not changed.
assumptions.text: Contested: the lesson teaches PI as the notes do, though String B's 1-minute readings are far above 5000 MΩ. IEEE 43 (a rotating-machine practice, research source 233) does not recommend PI above 5000 MΩ at 1 minute; the notes and Megger set no such limit for cables. The lesson says so, and the client's criterion and the trend settle it.

assumptions.label: PI and DAR bands: the notes' names are used
assumptions.why: Megger's Table I names PI below 1 dangerous, 1 to 2 questionable, 2 to 4 good, above 4 excellent, and DAR 1.0 to 1.25 questionable, 1.4 to 1.6 good, above 1.6 excellent with a gap between 1.25 and 1.4 (research sources 239, 240); a Megger Q&A calls PI 2.0 or higher and DAR 1.4 or higher good (sources 96, 97). The notes use poor, questionable, okay, good and DAR 1.25 and 1.6 with no gap (sources 26, 27). Practice readings are placed on the notes' bands; the others are shown as a maker's view.
assumptions.text: Contested: the lesson places String B on the notes' PI and DAR bands and shows Megger's Table I as a maker's different view (research sources 239, 240, 96, 97). The client's criterion settles pass or fail.

assumptions.label: The VLF voltage range: the notes' 1.5-2.5 U0 is used, and IEEE words it differently
assumptions.why: The notes give 1.5 to 2.5 U0 for installation, acceptance and maintenance (notes p.7). IEEE 400.2-2013 as reproduced by High Voltage Inc bases installation and acceptance levels on the most used worldwide practice 'from less than 2 U0 to 3U0', with maintenance about 75% of acceptance (research sources 108, 109); its 69 kV class row is 75, 84 and 63 kV rms for installation, acceptance and maintenance (source 112). At U0 = 38 kV the case spec of 2 U0 = 76 kV rms sits inside both the notes' range and the guide's row. The lesson teaches the notes' range and the guide's wording side by side; the client's specification settles the level.
assumptions.text: Contested: the VLF voltage range. The notes give 1.5 to 2.5 U0; IEEE 400.2 (as reproduced by High Voltage Inc) rests its installation and acceptance levels on practice of less than 2 U0 up to 3 U0 and sets maintenance at about 75% of acceptance (research sources 108, 109, 112). The client's specification settles it.

assumptions.label: A 66 kV array cable is withstand-tested at 0.1 Hz VLF in this case, though a resonant AC test is also used
assumptions.why: The notes and IEEE 400.2 (a guide for shielded cable rated 5 kV and above; its table stops at the 69 kV class) teach a 0.1 Hz VLF withstand (research sources 108, 116). A test-system maker reads IEC 63026 as requiring a test frequency of 10 to 500 Hz for commissioning cables above 36 kV (source 286), and a contractor tests 66 kV array strings with resonant test sets per IEC 63026 (sources 285, 287, 288). CIGRE TB 490, as quoted by INMR, accepts a lower frequency range down to 10 Hz for long submarine cables (source 289). The IEC 63026 clause text is paywalled and was not seen. The case follows the notes, with a client specification that asks for VLF, and the lesson tells Dan a 66 kV job's specification may call for a resonant AC test instead.
assumptions.text: Contested: whether VLF is the test for a 66 kV array cable. The notes and IEEE 400.2 teach 0.1 Hz VLF; a test-system maker says IEC 63026 asks for 10 to 500 Hz on cables above 36 kV, and resonant sets are used on 66 kV array strings (research sources 285-289). The clause itself was not seen, so the client's specification settles it. The case asks for VLF.

assumptions.label: The sheath test level: the notes' rule is used, and other levels exist
assumptions.why: The notes and IEC 60229 give 4 kV d.c. per mm of specified thickness, at most 10 kV, for 1 minute (research sources 29, 125). A network operator specifies 10 kV d.c. for 1 minute on new insulated-sheath cable and 5 kV for 1 minute on 6.6 to 33 kV polymeric cable (sources 247, 248); a cable maker's guide for medium-voltage cable uses a 1000 V insulation test (source 259). IEC 60840, whose range includes 66 kV, leaves submarine cables out of its scope and says the standard tests may need modifying (source 262). The case uses the notes' rule; the client's specification settles the level on a real job.
assumptions.text: Contested: the sheath test level. The notes and IEC 60229 give 4 kV per mm up to 10 kV for 1 minute; a network operator uses a flat 10 kV (5 kV on 6.6 to 33 kV polymeric cable); a cable maker's medium-voltage guide uses 1000 V; IEC 60840 leaves submarine cables out of its scope (research sources 29, 125, 247, 248, 259, 262). The case uses the notes' rule and the client's specification settles it.

assumptions.label: A sheath fault matters because water gets in and degrades the insulation over time
assumptions.why: The notes' added background (water treeing years later) is supported: water passing through a damaged sheath or joint causes water treeing under the electric field (research source 241); water trees grow over months or years until an electrical tree forms and the cable faults (sources 242, 243); moisture, a high field, defects and time promote them (source 244). A utility guide says failure does not follow a breach at once (source 246) and a commissioning review says failures are more often due to sheath problems than to the main insulation (source 263).
assumptions.text: Sourced: a sheath fault lets water in, and water trees grow in the insulation over months or years (research sources 241-244, 246, 263). The notes' added background holds.
